claims.claim: The page explains what happens when appropriated money is not spent

claims.claim: Impoundment, rescission and deferral are defined by the Impoundment Control Act of 1974
claims.sourceSpan: The Impoundment Control Act (ICA) amended the Antideficiency Act to limit its use for impounding funds and divided impoundments into two categories: deferrals, which provide for a temporary delay of spending, and rescissions, which provide for the permanent cancellation of spending.

claims.claim: There is a 45-day clock on withholding funds proposed for rescission
claims.sourceSpan: Any amount of budget authority proposed to be rescinded or that is to be reserved as set forth in such special message shall be made available for obligation unless, within the prescribed 45-day period, the Congress has completed action on a rescission bill rescinding all or part of the amount proposed to be rescinded or that is to be reserved.

claims.claim: Impoundment is appropriated funds withheld from obligation or expenditure
claims.sourceSpan: Impoundment occurs when appropriated funds are withheld from obligation or expenditure. Historically, most impoundments were noncontroversial, primarily undertaken to manage expenditures or effect savings.

claims.claim: The ICA followed President Nixon's assertion of unilateral withholding authority and the resulting litigation
claims.sourceSpan: In the 1970s, however, President Richard Nixon asserted the authority to act on his own to withhold funds or curtail programs he opposed. This assertion was challenged in the courts in a number of suits to compel the release of impounded funds or require the Administration to carry out statutory duties that would result in the expenditure of funds. Congress ultimately responded by enacting impoundment control legislation as Title X of the Congressional Budget and Impoundment Control Act of 1974 (P.L. 93-344).

claims.claim: GAO gives the same account of why the Act was passed
claims.sourceSpan: In 1974, Congress enacted the Impoundment Control Act in response to attempts by the executive branch to refuse to spend congressionally appropriated funds

claims.claim: The Act divided impoundments into deferrals and rescissions
claims.sourceSpan: The Impoundment Control Act (ICA) amended the Antideficiency Act to limit its use for impounding funds and divided impoundments into two categories: deferrals, which provide for a temporary delay of spending, and rescissions, which provide for the permanent cancellation of spending.

claims.claim: Before the ICA there was no express statutory limit on how long the President could withhold funds
claims.sourceSpan: Prior to the enactment of the ICA, there was no express statutory limit on the length of time the President could withhold appropriated funds.

claims.claim: Title X of the 1974 Act, codified at 2 U.S.C. 681-688, is the Impoundment Control Act
claims.sourceSpan: Title X of the Congressional Budget and Impoundment Control Act of 1974 (P.L. 93-344, 2 U.S.C. §§681-688) is known as the Impoundment Control Act (ICA).

claims.claim: The Act permits temporary impoundment on notice to Congress by special message
claims.sourceSpan: The act permits the President to temporarily impound

claims.claim: The Act provides for two types of impoundment
claims.sourceSpan: The Impoundment Control Act provides for two types of impoundments: deferrals and rescissions.

claims.field: Rescission vs. deferral: what's the difference?
claims.claim: A rescission is a proposed cancellation of budget authority before it would otherwise expire
claims.sourceSpan: A rescission is the proposed cancellation of budget authority that has been provided by Congress before that authority would otherwise expire.

claims.field: Rescission vs. deferral: what's the difference?
claims.claim: Funds may be withheld 45 days of continuous session, then must be released unless Congress completes action
claims.sourceSpan: Once a recission is proposed to Congress, the President can withhold the budget authority for 45 days while Congress is in continuous session. Unless Congress completes action on a rescission bill to approve the proposed rescission within that time, the budget authority must be made available for obligation.

claims.field: Rescission vs. deferral: what's the difference?
claims.claim: The statute states the release requirement and the 45-day period
claims.sourceSpan: Any amount of budget authority proposed to be rescinded or that is to be reserved as set forth in such special message shall be made available for obligation unless, within the prescribed 45-day period, the Congress has completed action on a rescission bill rescinding all or part of the amount proposed to be rescinded or that is to be reserved.

claims.field: Rescission vs. deferral: what's the difference?

claims.field: Rescission vs. deferral: what's the difference?
claims.claim: The statutory definition of deferral reaches executive action or inaction that effectively precludes obligation

claims.field: Rescission vs. deferral: what's the difference?
claims.claim: Deferrals are permissible only for contingencies, savings from changed requirements or efficiency, or as specifically provided by law, and for no other purpose
claims.sourceSpan: Deferrals shall be permissible only— (1) to provide for contingencies; (2) to achieve savings made possible by or through changes in requirements or greater efficiency of operations; or (3) as specifically provided by law. claims.sourceSpan: These procedures include limits on debate time, which effectively eliminates the need to invoke cloture to reach a final vote on the bill.

claims.claim: The Senate limit is not more than 10 hours on a rescission bill or impoundment resolution

claims.claim: REMOVED, F-FAIL (sweep, independently re-confirmed against CRS LSB11374): the dated-example box said the March 2025 preliminary injunction was "the first time a federal court addressed whether the executive may rely on the Impoundment Control Act's rescission-withholding provision to hold funds from obligation." It was not. CRS records that the March ruling rested on separation of powers and the APA "because the President had not then transmitted a special message under the ICA" - there was no rescission message to construe. The first judicial construction of Section 1012(b) is the SEPTEMBER 3, 2025 injunction, which CRS calls "the only judicial construction of Section 1012(b) to date."

REMOVED, F-FAIL found by this audit, not the sweep: the box said Chief Justice Roberts stayed "that injunction" - the March one. Two things are wrong with that. The March injunction had already been vacated in part by the D.C. Circuit on August 28, 2025, and the September 9 administrative stay was of the NEW preliminary injunction entered on September 3. The box is rebuilt as a dated chronology: March injunction, August 28 D.C. Circuit vacatur, August 28 special message, September 3 injunction, September 9 stay, undecided as of the source's last revision.

REMOVED, F-UNSOURCED, same class the senate-procedure and reconciliation pages fixed: "a qualifying rescission bill is considered under fast-track procedures, cannot be filibustered, and passes on a simple majority rather than the 60 votes cloture usually requires." The ICA changes no vote threshold. CRS R48432: "These procedures include limits on debate time, which effectively eliminates the need to invoke cloture to reach a final vote on the bill." The page now gives the actual figures from the statute - 10 hours in the Senate under 2 U.S.C. 688(d)(1), 2 hours in the House under 688(c)(2) - plus the germaneness bar and the CRS note that these are limits on debate, not on consideration. The parallel to reconciliation is now the sourced one: CRS calls the ICA language "analogous to the language in Title III of the Budget Act."

SOURCED, not removed (sweep Q-UNSOURCED): "The GAO has likened the maneuver to the line-item veto that the Supreme Court held unconstitutional in Clinton v. City of New York (1998)." The article's own cited GAO page does not say it - confirmed by a full read of the stored page. CRS LSB11374 does: GAO "likens pocket rescissions to the Line Item Veto Act of 1996, which the Supreme Court held unconstitutional in Clinton v. City of New York." Now attributed to CRS reporting GAO, and to the Line Item Veto Act of 1996 rather than a loose "line-item veto".

SOURCED, not removed (sweep Q-UNSOURCED): the entire paragraph attributing a legal position to OMB carried no citation anywhere on the page. CRS LSB11374 sets OMB's argument out in detail, including the comparison with the deferral provision and the Administration's answer to GAO's constitutional argument. The section now quotes CRS quoting OMB, with the speaker boundary marked.

SOURCED, not removed (sweep F-UNSOURCED, three items): "it checks that an impoundment is classified correctly ... and it can reclassify a message accordingly" and "The GAO is also directed to notify Congress if the President withholds funds without submitting the required special message." Both are now quoted from 2 U.S.C. 686(b) and 686(a) and from GAO's own page. The reclassification wording is corrected - the Comptroller General reports his reasons to both Houses; the statute does not give him power to reclassify the message himself. The 25-day precondition on a Comptroller General suit, which the page omitted entirely, is now quoted from 2 U.S.C. 687.

SOURCED, not removed (sweep U-FLAG): "After a series of disputes in the early 1970s over funds the executive branch declined to spend, Congress enacted the Impoundment Control Act of 1974." Replaced with the CRS R48432 account, which names the assertion, the litigation and the legislative response, plus GAO's parallel statement.

REMOVED, U-FLAG (sweep, four items): "That expedited path exists so Congress can act on a rescission request within the 45-day clock" (imputed legislative purpose); "Rescissions therefore differ from ordinary spending cuts in that they run through a defined statutory procedure"; "the fast-track, filibuster-proof treatment a rescission bill enjoys in the Senate parallels the expedited path used for budget reconciliation"; and "What ties them together is the constitutional starting point that spending authority comes from Congress." Replaced with sourced statements: the procedures are time-boxed to the withholding period, are not exclusive and are not required, and the reconciliation parallel is CRS's own "analogous to the language in Title III of the Budget Act."

REMOVED, S-RISK (sweep): "the question turns on contested points of statutory interpretation that, as of 2026, had been the subject of litigation but not settled by a final court ruling on the specific pocket-rescission question." Nothing stored supports a 2026 as-of date. The only source is a CRS Legal Sidebar last revised September 25, 2025, which says "The Court has not yet decided the application." Every claim in the litigation box is now dated to that revision, and the box says so in its own label.
